summary.summary: Cabinet re-presentation (4 August 2026) of the 2025/26 treasury outturn already seen by the Audit Committee on 24 June, now with the committee's minutes attached — and the minutes add material a lender should read. Borrowing rose £129.5m in one year to £713.5m, driven by capital spending, the need for exceptional financial support and continued lending into Medway Development Company, and the council is now £63m over-borrowed against its £650.5m borrowing CFR. Liquid treasury investments halved to £27m, the interest and financing budget overshot by £5.9m — partly because a budget-build error omitted some borrowing — and officers told members that Grant Thornton has had an MDC cashflow analysis for months without reaching a conclusion on the company's resilience. £20m of LOBO loans carry lender call options exercisable within 12 months.

signals.headline: 2025/26 borrowing growth of £129.5m (to £713.5m) attributed to capital spending, "the need for exceptional financial support" and Medway Development Company investment; minutes confirm net borrowing rose £118m with EFS a named driver
signals.why: The council is funding an EFS-supported revenue position with debt, so its budget balance depends on continued government permission and on the cost of that borrowing.

signals.headline: External borrowing £713.5m at 31 March 2026, up £129.5m in the year and £63.0m ABOVE the £650.5m borrowing CFR — the Audit Committee was told borrowing rose above the CFR partly to pre-fund monies owed to the council
signals.why: Borrowing beyond the underlying need means extra carrying cost and exposes the council to rate risk on cash it is waiting to recover.

signals.headline: Interest and Financing outturn £23.960m against an £18.107m budget — a £5.853m deficit, with interest paid £28.591m vs £22.381m budgeted after an error in the budget build omitted some borrowing
signals.why: A structural under-budgeting of debt costs that recurs into 2026/27 eats directly into revenue headroom.

signals.headline: £20m of LOBO loans have call dates within the next 12 months; officers estimate ~£60,000 extra cost if the most likely loan is called and ~£130,000 if all four (coupons 3.6%–4.75%) are called; a £10m Dexia LOBO was already repaid 26/09/25
signals.why: Calls would crystallise refinancing at today's higher rates on top of an already overspent financing budget.

signals.headline: £153.4m of loans to subsidiaries (long-term capital debtors £152.1m at 5.91%, up £36.6m in year, mainly Medway Development Company); Grant Thornton has been given an MDC cashflow analysis but "no conclusion had yet been reached" on its financial resilience
signals.why: A fifth of the council's debt is on-lent to a company whose resilience the external auditor has not yet been able to sign off.

signals.headline: Liquid treasury investments fell £25.2m in the year to £26.977m at 31 March 2026 (bank £0.1m, MMF £9.5m, property funds £17.4m) against £713.5m of borrowing
signals.why: Under 4% investment cover against the debt book leaves little cash buffer if short-term rollover or LOBO calls arrive together.

compliance.notes: Strong on the core prudential/treasury mechanics: an exemplary liability benchmark charted to ~2094, a fully year-on-year-reconciled CFR, a sophisticated MUFG creditworthiness policy (ratings+CDS), a full-council MRP statement over asset life, and a complete TMP suite (incl a nine-risk TMP1 and an ESG policy). Weakest area is the commercial/non-treasury investment disclosures given a material service/commercial book (MDC loans up to 120m, property funds): no proportionality/headroom test (COM-03), no paras 51-53 compliance statement (COM-02), no IMPs (COM-05), and the new commercial-income prudential indicator (PI-08) is not set. Also missing: audit-qualification flag (RPT-05) and third-party/pension-monies attribution (GOV-07). Notable risk read: 31% of the 639m debt book is short-term (<1yr) borrowing with ~225m more new borrowing planned to 2028/29 - the TMPs themselves flag the elevated refinancing risk.

news_drafts.headline: Medway faces £26.7m current-year overspend and £65m structural deficit dependent on government funding
news_drafts.lead: Medway Council faces a £26.7m overspend forecast in the current financial year, exceeding its total general reserves of £10.1m, and a structural budget gap of £65.9m in 2027/28 rising to £359.3m cumulatively across the medium term. The financial plan cannot be balanced without exceptional financial support from government—permission to borrow to cover day-to-day spending—which has not been confirmed for 2027/28. If the government refuses, the Section 151 officer, the council's chief finance officer, may be forced to issue a Section 114 notice, a formal warning that the council cannot balance its budget, which freezes new spending until councillors agree a plan. The Cabinet heard pressures of £38.6m in adult social care and £9.2m in children's services, with adult social care costs having more than doubled since 2020-21.

findings.headline: Children's Services facing £9.210m increase with 50 new placements and 21 external residential placements at £6,001-£9,000 per week, plus 9% SEND transport growth.
findings.detail: Children's Social Care requires £9.210m additional funding in 2027/28. Demographic change drives 50 new placements at £2.202m cost. Current service cost pressure of £4.444m reflects existing caseload. The Council currently has 21 External Residential placements at weekly costs between £6,001-£9,000 (2026 prices) and a further 21 at £3,001-£6,000. Education faces SEND transport growth of 9% with cost per pupil increasing by approximately £6,000 since June 2024. Both are demand-driven with current caseload already very high-cost.
findings.matters: Children's services are demand-driven and the council has statutory duty to fund them. Very high-cost placements (£9,000/week) are major individual line items. Demographic growth means this will continue to escalate.
findings.figures: £9.210m increase 2027/28; 50 new placements at £2.202m cost; currently 21 external residential placements at £6,001-£9,000/week and 21 at £3,001-£6,000/week; SEND transport growth 9%; cost per pupil increased £6,000 since June 2024
findings.quote: The primary driver is the change in demographics which show an increase of 50 placements at a cost of £2.202million in 2027/28. Further to this an increase of £4.444million is projected for the current cost of service pressure...Further to the above, the increase in the number of children in higher cost placements seen to date in 2026/27 is also reflected...there are 21 External Residential placements at a weekly cost between £6,001 - £9,000 current and a further 21 in placements costing between £3,001 - £6,000.

findings.headline: Council is using one-off asset sales (£8m in 2027/28, tapering to £1.5m by 2029/30) to fund interest and financing costs, masking the underlying structural problem.
findings.detail: The Interest and Financing budget includes a projected saving of £8m in 2027/28 from 'capital receipts from sale of investment properties'. Further asset sale receipts of £2m (2028/29) and £1.5m (2029/30) are assumed. This is a one-off measure; once investment properties are sold, they cannot be sold again. Using asset sales to fund operating costs is a sign of financial distress and reduces the sustainability of the budget solution.
findings.matters: A lender needs to distinguish between sustainable and one-off cost reductions. Asset sales to fund revenue operations cannot continue indefinitely. This suggests the true structural deficit is larger than the headline figures and the council is drawing down its asset base.
findings.figures: £8m saving from asset sales 2027/28; £2m in 2028/29; £1.5m in 2029/30
findings.quote: Interest & Financing - Saving on I&F budget due to capital receipts from sale of investment properties 8,000   2,000  1,500  1,500

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation costs projected to increase by £3.8m in 2027/28 with demand growing at unsustainable 10% annually, compounding current-year £1.6m overspend.
findings.detail: Temporary Accommodation costs are forecast to rise by £3.8m in 2027/28. Principal driver is continued reliance on nightly-paid private landlord accommodation, pressured by both increasing number of households requiring TA and higher costs charged by providers. Current year (2026/27) already shows in-year pressure of £1.6m against approved budget. The service proposes baseline growth assumption of 10% for 2027/28. Further work is underway to 'ensure that the 2027/28 budget is appropriately rebased', suggesting the full extent of the underlying cost is not yet quantified.
findings.matters: Temporary Accommodation is demand-driven by homelessness and therefore difficult to control through efficiency. The 10% annual growth is unsustainable and indicates a deepening crisis the council cannot manage. Already showing in-year overspend in current year.
findings.figures: £3.8m additional pressure 2027/28; £1.6m in-year overspend forecast 2026/27; 10% annual growth assumption
findings.quote: A further significant pressure relates to Temporary Accommodation (TA) costs of £3.800 million. The principal cost driver is the continued use of nightly paid accommodation provided by private landlords...Round 1 revenue budget monitoring for 2026/27 forecast an in-year pressure of £1.6 million against the approved budget...The service has reviewed demand and expenditure trends over the previous two years and proposes a baseline growth assumption of 10% for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Council depends on Exceptional Financial Support from Government, not yet confirmed for 2027/28; if refused, Section 151 officer may be forced to issue Section 114 notice.
findings.detail: The MTFO explicitly states that 'The current MTFO projections cannot be balanced through the use of reserves and assume that further exceptional financial support from Government will be required.' The Chief Operating Officer is engaged in ongoing discussions with MHCLG, and the Deputy Leader has written to the Secretary of State requesting additional grant funding. The risk register rates the scenario of EFS refusal as 'D1' (Rare/Critical) and notes: 'In the unlikely event that the MHCLG rejects the Council's latest application for EFS, the Section 151 Officer may be forced to issue a Section 114 notice to the Council.' A Section 114 notice effectively declares the authority unable to set a balanced budget.
findings.matters: The council's financial plan is not self-balancing; it depends on government support that has not yet been confirmed for future years. A lender needs to know whether this support is reliably available. Section 114 notices are rare and mark authorities as in formal financial difficulty.
findings.figures: £65.858m 2027/28 gap dependent on EFS; EFS already granted for 2025/26 (£9.856m) and agreed in-principle for 2026/27 (total £28.003m borrowed)
findings.quote: The current MTFO projections cannot be balanced through the use of reserves and assume that further exceptional financial support from Government will be required. There remains a significant risk to the Council's financial resilience should additional support not be forthcoming...In the unlikely event that the MHCLG rejects the Council's latest application for EFS, the Section 151 Officer may be forced to issue a Section 114 notice to the Council.

findings.headline: General reserves of £10.012m represent less than 2% of budget, materially below prudent level of 5%, with no capacity to absorb further financial shocks.
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2027, the Council is projected to hold £10.012m in general reserves. This represents less than 2% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget and is materially below levels typically regarded as prudent. The Section 151 Officer has set an aspiration to build reserves to 5% of budget (c£25m) to provide adequate safety net. The medium-term outlook reflects contribution of £5m per year from revenue budget to rebuild reserves, but this assumes balanced budgets are achieved, which they are not projected to be.
findings.matters: Reserves are critical buffer against financial shocks and unforeseen pressures. At less than 2%, Medway has almost no protection. The current-year £26.7m overspend already exceeds reserves. The rebuilding plan assumes the underlying budget problems are solved, which they are not.
findings.figures: £10.012m reserves at 31 March 2027; less than 2% of net revenue budget; aspiration £25m (5%); gap of £15m to reach prudent level
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2027, the Council is projected to hold £10.012million in general reserves. The General Reserves balance therefore represents less than 2% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget, which is materially below the level typically regarded as prudent for an authority facing the degree of financial risk reflected within this MTFO.
